Setup: payoff for position a ∈ [-1,1], hold one minute: net = aY − k|a|. Conditional mean μ = E[Y|x] lies in [m̂−u, m̂+u], conditional variance fixed v > 0. Robust objective (worst-case mean, penalty lam a² v/2 as a risk/penalty term):

F(a) = min_{μ∈[m̂−u,m̂+u]} { a μ − k|a| − λ a² v/2 }.

Since aμ is linear in μ, min attained at endpoint: μ = m̂ − u if a ≥ 0, μ = m̂ + u if a ≤ 0.

Define robust long edge R₊ = m̂ − u − k and robust short edge R₋ = −m̂ − u − k. Then F(a) = a R₊ − λ a² v/2 for a ≥ 0 and = (−a) R₋ − λ a² v/2 for a ≤ 0. Actually for a ≤ 0, set b = −a: F = b R₋ − λ b² v/2. Symmetric.

Maximize each branch: unconstrained b* = R/(λ v); constrained b̂ = clip(R/(λ v), 0, 1). Value V(R) = if R ≤ 0: 0 attained at b=0; else with c = λ v: b̂ = min(R/c, 1); V = R b̂ − c b̂²/2 = R²/(2c) if R ≤ c, else R − c/2.

F(0)=0. So a* = +b̂₊ if V₊ > max(V₋, 0); −b̂₋ if V₋ > max(V₊,0); 0 in case of a tie or nonpositive edges. Strict inequality required to trade ("no-trade tie" → a=0).

Special cases:
- λ = 0: F is linear on each branch; max at b = 1 whenever R > 0. a* = +1 if R₊>0 and R₊>R₋; −1 if R₋>0 and R₋>R₊; 0 otherwise (including ties and zero edges). Both edges positive is impossible for k ≥ 0, u ≥ 0: R₊ + R₋ = −2(u+k) ≤ 0.
- u = 0: reduces to standard certainty-equivalent-ish solution a = clip((m̂−k)/(λ v),0,1) etc.
- If λ v is small, saturation at |a|=1.

Threshold interpretation with λ>0: trade long iff R₊ > 0 i.e. m̂ > u + k; short iff m̂ < −(u+k). The interval half-width acts like an extra cost buffer. Note also for λ>0, if both V₊ and V₋ positive (can't both be given R₊+R₋ ≤ 0? Actually both positive requires R₊>0 and R₋>0 which is impossible) so at most one branch active; tie can only occur when both values zero → a=0. So ties essentially reduce to zero edges. But implement tie handling anyway (exact float equality of branch values → 0).

Actually careful: can V₊ == V₋ > 0? Requires both R>0 — impossible. So ties only at 0. Good.

Note the max-min is a max over a of min over μ — the order: max_a min_μ. Yes.

Also mention: the "risk" penalty λ a² v/2 uses the same v as the conditional variance; with fixed v it acts as a quadratic size penalty. If lam=0, no risk penalty; solution bang-bang.

What is guaranteed / not if true model falls outside interval: If true μ ∉ [m̂−u, m̂+u], the min-max guarantee vanishes: the chosen a maximizes the worst case only over the assumed set; if the true μ is outside, the realized expected net a μ − k|a| can be negative even though the robust value F(a*) ≥ 0. Nothing about tails, variance mis-specification, cost mis-specification, or execution guarantees. Also the whole thing is conditional on correctness of the model class (linear conditional mean), correct u calibration (requires iid Gaussian homoskedastic exogenous errors), and correctness of v and k. Robustness is only to μ within the interval — not to variance, distributional, dependence, or cost uncertainty. If μ outside the interval, expected net can be as low as... e.g., a* = 1 case: expected net = μ − k which could be −∞ in principle; no bound. Also note the flat position a=0 always guarantees exactly 0 net, so the robust formulation never does worse than 0 in worst case over the assumed set (F(a*) ≥ 0), but outside the set even that comparison can invert.

Interval distinctions: u(x) is a pointwise conditional-mean interval from the t-distribution under exact OLS assumptions; new-observation prediction interval half-width adds +1 inside the sqrt (s√(1 + 1/n + (x−x̄)²/Sxx)). Prediction interval targets a single future y = μ(x) + ε including noise; the mean interval targets μ(x) and is much narrower.

Coverage caveat: the count of validation y inside the prediction intervals is an empirical check of prediction-interval calibration (for observations), not of the conditional mean. The conditional mean μ(x) is unobserved — a single y at each x is one draw of noise; you cannot measure coverage of μ(x) from y coverage. Conversely the narrow mean interval containing y only 14% of the time is expected (y includes noise), and the99.9% prediction coverage here reflects over-wide s from train (variance regime shift), not valid mean coverage.
